issues.text: We found no measured results from Georgia high schools yet.
issues.issue: The same data-gap caveat now differs by side. Card 1 (supports) ends 'We found no measured results from Georgia high schools yet.' Card 5 (opposes, L201) lost 'yet' in 6.4 when 'measured' was added to stay at 40 words: 'We found no measured Georgia high school results or workload data.' So the supporters' missing data reads as on its way, and the opponents' reads as simply missing. Both cards' labels and 'What's uncertain' fields still say 'yet'.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop 'yet' from card 1's In short (34 words) so both read 'We found no measured ...'. Or restore 'yet' on card 5 and trim one word there to stay within 40.

issues.text: Schools must enforce the ban. [P-014] Staff policing phones can invite conflict, opponents say. [P-047, P-071]
issues.issue: Card 5's In short puts only the conflict half of its claim in opponents' terms. The burden half (Adams: the bill 'would put the burden on teachers and administrators to police phones', P-047; the card title says 'will burden school staff') is only implied by 'Staff policing phones' and the closing 'workload data'. So the evidence-status sentence answers a claim the line never states. Flip test: both supporters' predictive In shorts state the whole claim with 'would' ('Students would learn more', 'would improve'). The opponents' only predictive In short states its claim only with 'can'. Each modal matches its source, but choosing which half to state is our edit.
issues.suggested_fix: Within 40 words: 'Schools must enforce the ban. [P-014] That burdens staff and can invite conflict, opponents say. [P-047, P-071] A Florida study found enforcement led to more suspensions at first, especially among Black students. [P-039] We found no measured Georgia high school results or workload data. {analysis: unchanged}'

issues.text: High school students should be allowed to keep phone access, opponents say, because teens are older and often more independent and the choice should be parents'.
issues.issue: This is the only In short whose attribution sits mid-sentence, before a 'because' clause. A reader can take the reasons, including 'the choice should be parents'', as the page's own explanation of why opponents say it. That would put 'should' in our voice. The other five cards attribute at the end of the claim, so their whole claim is clearly the side's.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the reasons part of what opponents say: 'High school students should be allowed to keep phone access, opponents say: teens are older and often more independent, and the choice should be parents'.' Citations stay the same, and the line is 31 words with 'The disagreement is mainly about values.'

issues.text: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: how much work enforcement takes; the law sets aside no money, and we didn't review the state budget.
issues.issue: The staff line gives the no-money caveat alone. Elsewhere the page pairs it with the state's support duty: Option B says 'The law gives schools state guidance but sets aside no money', and card 5 says 'the state must give them guidance and technical support' (P-016). For staff, whose line is about enforcement, leaving out P-016 means the line shows only the burden. The caveat's punctuation also no longer matches the parent line's (parentheses since 6.4).
issues.suggested_fix: 'Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: how much work enforcement takes. The law gives schools state guidance but sets aside no money; we didn't review the state budget.' Reuse Option B's tag: {analysis: no funding provision in the full enacted text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061; P-016 provides guidance; the budget is outside our sources}. Use the same caveat form as the parent line.

issues.text: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: who pays for phone storage (the law sets aside no money; we didn't review the state budget).
issues.issue: 'Who pays' assumes storage costs something, but P-009's options include a student's locker or a set place in the classroom. The page's 'Not known yet' bullet (L31) asks the same question without that assumption: 'whether that costs families anything'. Asked as 'who pays', the parent's one unknown starts from a cost.
issues.suggested_fix: 'Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: whether phone storage will cost families anything (the law sets aside no money; we didn't review the state budget).' The tag stays the same.

flip_test.flipped: From the supporters' side a student line might say 'your school day will be phone-free'. From the opponents' side it might say 'you lose your phone all day'. The line does neither. It states the rule ('you can't access') and the exceptions in the law's terms, then the unknown start date.
flip_test.asymmetry: none. 'Only' reflects P-013's 'as necessary to fulfill the requirements' limit, which the tag quotes. It is not a tilt.

flip_test.flipped: The first sentence avoids both sides' framings ('phone-free day' and 'lose direct contact') and states P-011's two duties. The unknown, though, is asked cost-first. In the neutral form the page uses at L31, it would read 'whether phone storage will cost families anything'.
flip_test.asymmetry: minor: 'who pays' assumes a cost (see issue). Together with L16, cost is the only kind of unknown the parent and staff lines raise. The contested benefits are covered in L33 and Layer 4, which is acceptable for this practical section.

flip_test.flipped: The line uses neither the opponents' framing ('staff must police phones') nor the supporters' ('teachers can just teach again', P-045). It states P-014's duties. Using the page's own Option B pairing, its caveat would read '... the law gives schools state guidance but sets aside no money'.
flip_test.asymmetry: minor: the no-money caveat appears without the state-support fact (P-016) that Option B and card 5 pair it with (see issue).

flip_test.flipped: Neither side's: it describes what HB 1009 keeps and changes for K-8 and makes no claim for either side.
flip_test.asymmetry: none. 'Incomplete' is accurate to P-004's 'includes, but is not limited to'. 'Open-ended' would avoid any hint that the list is a drafting flaw.

flip_test.flipped: The lead-in covers both lines equally: same survey, same sample, same description.

'If you care most about reaching your child in an emergency: In the Emory survey, the top reason parents cited for opposing a high school cellphone ban was "No way to reach child during emergency."' This is L106 word for word.
flip_test.asymmetry: none. Same form, source, verb ('cited') and quote position. Lengths are 32 and 35 words, with quotes of 5 and 7 words. No recommendation words. The heading narrows the quote to 'focus'. That keeps 'learning', which opposing parents also invoke ('Phones needed for schoolwork', 'Students need to learn responsible use', P-035), from going to one side only. 'Backing' is a plain synonym of the survey's 'Supporting'.

flip_test.flipped: 'If you care most about your child's focus in class: In the Emory survey, the top reason parents cited for backing a high school cellphone ban was "Improved academic focus and learning."' This is L105 word for word.
flip_test.asymmetry: none. The heading names opposing parents' specific concern, reaching a child. It does not claim safety in general, which supporting parents also cite ('Improved physical health and safety', 60.3%, P-034), so the shared-value rule holds. The emergency heading carries more emotional weight than 'focus in class', but it is that side's own top reason. Toning it down to match would misstate their value.

flip_test.flipped: 'Option X has no line because we found no documented argument for it.' This reads the same for any option without a documented argument.

Card 5's mirror: '... A Florida study found enforcing bans led to more suspensions at first, especially among Black students. We found no measured Georgia high school results or workload data.' Both use the same study verbs ('found ... led to'). Each has a timing qualifier ('second year' / 'at first'). Neither mentions that the study is a working paper.
flip_test.asymmetry: caveat wording: card 1's data-gap sentence ends with 'yet' and card 5's no longer does (see issue). Otherwise parallel.

flip_test.flipped: 'A study in England found no evidence of [the other side's predicted effect] ... That study couldn't test cause and effect.' This reads the same. The caveat follows the study's design, not the side, and the page attaches it wherever the England study is used (Options A and B).

'[An opponents' factual claim], opponents say. Our sources give statements, not measured results.' This reads the same. Card 4 carries the equivalent 'no data' caveat, and card 5 has 'no measured ... data'.

'Under the law, students can't access phones during the day. [A supporters' claim], supporters say. Our sources have no data on ...' Card 4 opens in our voice with the law's text, and no supporters' card has an equivalent. That follows the evidence: the law's text backs only card 4's factual half. Since 6.4, the attribution verb and its end position match cards 1-3 and 5.
flip_test.asymmetry: none (follows the sources). P-071 reports supporters' 'would' and opponents' 'could', and the cards keep each side's own modal.

flip_test.flipped: Card 1 rewritten in card 5's shape would read 'Schools must ban phones. Fewer phones can help students learn, supporters say. ...', which is weaker than the actual 'Students would learn more with fewer distractions, supporters say.' Card 5 states the duty in our voice and only the 'can invite conflict' half in opponents' terms. The burden half is implied. 'Especially among Black students' and 'enforcing bans' (not 'phone bans') follow P-039, so they are not asymmetries.
flip_test.asymmetry: low: the claim is less complete and its modal weaker than in cards 1-2, and the line lacks card 1's 'yet' (see issues).

flip_test.flipped: A supporters' card in this shape ('[claim], supporters say, because [reasons]. The disagreement is mainly about values.') would read the same.
flip_test.asymmetry: structural only: this is the one In short with mid-sentence attribution followed by a 'because' clause. A reader can take the reasons, including 'the choice should be parents'', as ours (see issue). Listing reasons fits a values claim, so that part is not a tilt.

summary: The values guide mirrors cleanly (same survey, form and verb, 32 and 35 words, no recommendation words, no shared value given to one side), and the 'In short' lines share the attribution verb, parallel Florida wording on both sides and a data caveat on every card. The remaining asymmetries are all low (card 1 keeps a 'yet' that card 5 lost, card 5 states only the 'can invite conflict' half of its claim, card 6's attribution sits before a 'because' clause, and the parent and staff 'If you' unknowns frame storage and enforcement as costs without the page's neutral or paired wording), and page.yaml's title and chips raise no balance issue.
